headline: A 2017 law that sets research, science education, and technology rules for federal agencies such as NSF, NIST, and OSTP, mostly by directing them to study, coordinate, or run programs.
what_it_does: The law covers many science and technology topics across six titles. It tells the National Science Foundation to keep its merit review criteria, to fund research and education grants, and to add oversight to major research facility projects. It directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to research cybersecurity, quantum-resistant cryptography, and the security of voting systems, and to run its manufacturing and apprenticeship-related programs. It also asks the Office of Management and Budget to reduce paperwork for federally funded researchers and lets agencies use crowdsourcing and citizen science.

who_it_affects.group: Researchers who receive federal science grants
who_it_affects.how: They face a planned effort to reduce administrative paperwork and a review of required progress reports.

who_it_affects.group: Students and institutions in STEM fields
who_it_affects.how: The National Science Foundation must award grants to broaden participation by underrepresented groups and to support computer science education.
Commerce must study the cost of creating apprenticeship programs, especially for small businesses, and may work with Labor on ways to reduce it.
The Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership, which helps manufacturers, has its requirements revised.
NIST may research the security of computers and networks used in voting systems.

who_it_affects.group: Undergraduate students at colleges and universities
who_it_affects.how: Each federal agency must recommend ways to expand research opportunities for them.

when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law on January 6, 2017; most provisions direct agencies to act over time, and specific deadlines vary by section.
